items.body: Artwork by Natasha at Aza Nizi Maza And we are back after the summer break with a new episode of UFN. I wish Ukraine could have had a bit of a break as well, but far from it. Ballistic missile attacks have only intensified, while Kramatorsk and Slovyansk increasingly resemble ghost towns. This month we introduce several new voices to the UFN universe, including Aircraft, whom I had the pleasure of meeting in Berlin back in June; Bey O Bey from Kyiv, praising the level of organisation in smaller cities such as Khmelnytskyi and Vinnytsia; TRANCEDÆNCE, referencing the work of Mark Fisher; and Соня Хедекель [Sofiia Khedekel], who is starting to forget what life was like before the full-scale invasion in Kharkiv. Furthermore, Roksana Smirnova and Misha Kalinin imagine the moment after the war ends in Tallinn, and Forma Formanta, in Kyiv, discusses freedom. We are also very pleased to reconnect with old friends Bohdan Stupak, Fedir Tkachov and Lu Joyce, as well as the Sumy-based label Bondeni through Kateryna Pavlovska, all talking to us about their new releases. There’s a big crop of new music, including a double fundraisier by Side-Line Magazine and releases by Alexander Stratonov, Alla Zagaykevych, Ambiotik, Corn Wave, Cryptic Chorus, Decorodi, Doctor Bugg, Horizon Resonances, Khladna Landscape, Kotra, Mootney, Motorpig, Neroba, Oleksii Podat, Peshka, Piriinka, Regina Collage, Ross Khmil, Sasha Chemerov & Hidden Element, Tetiana Khoroshun, v4w.enko, Valentin Silvestrov, ХЖВИ, Ніщо, Vøvk, КАТ, Serhii Litinskyi, DJ POPS and 58918012. In the mix section, we have new sets by Vlad Fisun, Bogdan Zaiets, Ecce Lizard, Reshat and Khrystyna Kirik. In the viewing room, we have videos by Natalia Tsupryk, Ignea, Vera Logdanidi and Zavoloka, alongside a new documentary by Suspilne about Ukrainian children being adopted in Italy under the guise of the international principle of “the best interests of the child”. We also feature a DJ set by Ro_Ma 4E (Roman Cherkas), a veteran who took up DJing thanks to EnterDJ and performed at one of the Czech Republic’s most popular festivals, Colours of Ostrava, back in July. And to finish proceedings, a set by Vlad Fisun. Daryna But first, this month’s Resonance FM podcast features Daryna, a 16-year-old girl from Kharkiv, talking about the art studio Aza Nizi Maza, founded by Mykola Kolomyets in 2012 and working creatively with children with disabilities and those on the autism spectrum. The studio has continued to operate throughout the full-scale invasion, becoming both a haven for creativity and a reference point for foreign journalists seeking to understand life in Kharkiv. During our conversation, we discussed the studio’s ethos, the language issue, and what everyday life is like for schoolchildren in Kharkiv, where classes are now conducted online and students meet physically once a week, with only a limited number actually attending in person. Aza Nizi Maza Studio Tracklist: headachee – хедейк Соня Хедекель – Унісон SadSvit – Той, хто пісню грав REGINA COLLAGE – Горизонт ХЖВИ – Они все nearr – Календар СТРУКТУРА ЩАСТЯ – Лесбіянство (не) модно Zhadan, Ojra, Kiritchenko – Чорнотроп Dirtbag Loris – Праска   JULY 21, 2026 – BERLIN photo by @yaroslavstorchak Aircraft Your latest album, Тигролови, marks a return to singing entirely in Ukrainian, and even its visual identity draws on the work of the celebrated Ukrainian folk artist Mariya Prymachenko, whose paintings have become powerful cultural symbols in recent years. Before discussing the record itself, could you introduce yourself to our readers and tell us about your musical background? What led you to start making music as Aircraft, and why did returning to the Ukrainian language—and to these distinctly Ukrainian visual and cultural references—feel important for this album? Hi, I started Aircraft 15 years ago as a side lo-fi project which eventually grew up to what it is now. My background was mainly grunge then garage-punk music, I played in several bands, including Buzzmonster, Martiansdoitbetter, The Dontpaniks. I just fell in love with delays in reverbs at some point and switched to more postpunk sound. Ukrainian was always big for me, I was listening mainly to Ukrainian or Western music. And before pro-russian dictator Yanukovich – Ukrainian was very big in underground. For example in 2008-2010 we were singing mainly Ukrainian. Then russia took it from us, pouring billions in propaganda of russian culture. Before Ukrainian was developing quite rapidly. So now it is a third renesanse on my memory of Ukrainian language – 90’s then 2000s then 2014-now. So as an artist i feel responsibility to work with Ukrainian audience, also exporting our culture, and cultural code abroad. Your lyrics often rely on deceptively simple images—night, forests, birds, wire, winter—that gradually accumulate emotional weight without ever becoming overtly symbolic. “Мавĸа” (Mavka) draws on Ukrainian folklore while remaining firmly grounded in the emotional reality of the present, while “Люди” (People) and “Зона” (The Zone) evoke displacement through remarkably economical language. How do songs usually begin for you? Do they emerge first from words, melodies, or atmospheres? I think from memories, by actualising them we create future and hope. That what my music is about. The album repeatedly returns to the idea of waiting. In “Гаю Час” (Killing Time), waiting becomes almost a state of existence, while “Навĸоло Ніч” (Night All Around) transforms the night into a space where time seems suspended altogether. These songs avoid political slogans, yet the war is present in every silence and every hesitation. Was it important for you to write about the psychological consequences of war rather than documenting events directly? I don’t agree that it doesn’t have political slogans, I say, “I will never forgive the world when the war is over”. Which means the passiveness of western politicians, often loyal to russia, fossil fuels dependancy instead of protection etc. Tons of hypocrisy. That is quite political I think. What does it mean for you to be Ukrainian and if you had to pick a film, novel, artwork, building, dish, song, album, and meme that best represents Ukraine for you at present what would you choose? Emm. I don’t like this question. I would rather answer what does it mean to be a Ukrainian artist. It is picking the hardest themes to work with. Developing fast, by accepting harsh reality as it is. Struggling being “too authentic” in the standartized and refined European industry. A lot of distributors, streaming platforms and music businesses in general still recognise the post soviet map as one environment, which is ridiculous, since it hasn’t existed for 40 years. Which smells like chauvinism to me. All in all I think there is still quite a lot of that in Europe. As a Ukrainian and a Ukrainian artist I faced it a lot. And we now pay for our recognition a very high price. However, I always see bright lights of hope here and there, and your project is one of them. So thank you!   AUGUST 12, 2026 – KYIV Bohdan Stupak Hi Bohdan, when we spoke back in 2024, you said that the full-scale invasion had made you realise you needed “a stronger voice” for your story to be heard, and much of your work at the time—war.datapoints, Voices of War, “air raid siren is over”—dealt quite directly with the sonic reality of war. Since then, book of sorrow and a place in memories seem to turn inward, towards beauty, memory, loss and contemplation. What has changed for you over these two years, both personally and as an artist? Is this retreat from explicitly war-related material a consequence of the fatigue you describe in the notes to book of sorrow, or does it represent a more fundamental change in what you now want music to do? Surely, there is fatigue present. Nobody expected that the war would drag on for more than 4 years. And one cannot stay constantly alert for such a long time. But also, a lot of things happened in my personal life. Getting to know loss, grief. And the art was always a great therapeutic way to process such strong feelings. But most importantly, although now I’m dealing with more “neutral” subjects, people from other countries still ask me about what it is like being a Ukrainian nowadays and ask me a lot about life in Ukraine. So I guess, working with such universal topics still allows me to raise the voice I dreamed of, although in softer ways. Back then, circumstances had forced you to leave your guitar in Kyiv, and you told me that you hoped eventually to bring organic sounds back into your music. book of sorrow almost feels like the fulfilment of that wish: the entire record was made from a single guitar, processed until it can resemble horns, strings or an ensemble, while drawing on Baroque harmony and the European classical tradition. Why did you impose this restriction on yourself, particularly after working so extensively with SuperCollider, algorithms, field recordings and data? It is not like I imposed the restriction. It’s rather that I was so mesmerised with the sound that I got, that I felt that nothing else was needed! Of course, with “a place in memories”, I had to move further and incorporate this type of sound into my entire system of program-generated textures. And did rediscovering the guitar change the way you thought about composition? I wouldn’t say that it was a dramatic change, but rather a gradual process that happened over the years. With my first project “fractions” I explored the entire sonic field with the means of numbers. But when “grammars” arrived, I felt I had to find the link between beauty and the algorithm. So now, when I have a guitar at my disposal, I have another powerful instrument I can augment the algorithm with. There is an interesting progression from book of sorrow to a place in memories. On the former you write about seeking beauty as nourishment during a period of exhaustion, although war inevitably remains present beneath the music; on the latter, memory itself becomes the subject, beginning with your recollection of the Black Sea in 2017 and the recognition that an occupied part of Ukraine now exists for you less as a geographical place than as “a certain point in the past”. How do you distinguish memory from nostalgia here? It’s a great word “nostalgia”. I think it was the missing word that would neatly describe the music when I was writing one-sheet for it. And I think it’s great that this is nostalgia, not just memory, as listeners seek emotion, not the documentality. When a place still exists physically but has become inaccessible through occupation, does remembering it alter the meaning of both place and time? It is a hard question. On the one hand, the place would be special anyways because of that special time we had there, which we can never bring back. But on the other hand, I feel bitterness every time I think that those places are not only physically inaccessible now but also plundered (like Askania Nova natural reserve). A lot of people are already nostalgic for the first months of the war, the first blackouts. There’s a growing pull toward more conventional hauntological gestures — artists sampling Ukrainian pop from the 2000s, grieving lost national futures against the futures Russia tried to promise us instead. Stalker 2 is a good example of how the discourse has shifted since the invasion — the relationship to lost futures there is much more contradictory and tangled than the classic version, closer to how I think Ukrainian collective memory actually works now. We can’t separate ourselves from these missing meanings — not just ideas about a better past or future, but ideas about what being Ukrainian even is. We still need to fight for our present and build a future, but these lost futures and broken pasts have become part of the cultural fabric for a lot of Ukrainians, so I think there’s real, useful work to do with them — using older hauntological tools and building new ones. My own practice has become more centered on hauntology over the last couple of years — “Missing Sounds” among other pieces — and I think I get closer to something meaningful when I try new mediums and methods rather than just sampling or referencing symbols that trigger nostalgia. I’m also finding new ways of noticing my own hauntological code — ghosts I didn’t know I was carrying — in landscape, architecture, sound, local communities, time itself, food, language, products. want those new perspectives to actually do something — to build more promising, more emancipated versions of reality, not just describe the loss. Administration, recorded across 2023, reduces its accompanying text to two words—“drug / politics”—and titles its pieces “Blackout”, “Boise” and “Brothel”. Then Dnipro City Guardian gives us “Taking a Dump at Biennale Restroom”, “DCCC” and “Haunt of Kaminya”. There seems to be a mixture of seriousness, absurdity and private mythology running through these titles. How autobiographical is TRANCEDÆNCE, and how much are you constructing a fictional world around experiences that actually happened? That’s something I think about myself a lot as of recently. I’ve been doing more institutional artist practices and started signing my works with my real name Oleksandr Suprun more frequently, and I’ve realized I can use both names — TRANCEDÆNCE and my real name — more or less interchangeably, depending on what the work needs. From the start of the project I saw TRANCEDÆNCE as whatever musical or sound work I do inside contemporary art and institutional avant-garde music. I still construct and work on the overall artist identity and design of this project to build some cohesive artistic statement. But I see TRANCEDÆNCE as less autobiographical or focused on narrative world-building and much more about conceptual depth and the listener’s own subjective reading — emotional states, psychological associations, that kind of thing. I try to keep things as abstract, vague, and surreal as I can; what a track title looks and sounds like as a combination of letters, or what colors go on the artwork, usually matters more to me than sending any specific message. That said, I can see the project moving toward more worldbuilding or a more unified narrative in specific works, even if that’s not really the focus. With Dnipro City Guardian the album got more personal and specific than anything before it — I wanted to say something about my hometown and its local identity, and for the first time in my career I felt genuinely connected to that. It was a shift for me as much as for the music. I want TRANCEDÆNCE to be open to such dynamics and only be limited to this electroacoustic improvisation praxis I was talking about earlier. The mythos side of things — private mythology, world-building, a constructed persona — is something I work with much more directly under my other alias, Cynpym, which I use for my blog, more conventional music, poetry, graphic work, and my main social presence. I try to keep the two as genuinely separate mindsets and workflows. It’s honestly a challenge right now: TRANCEDÆNCE ended up giving me a functional method and became the direction my career moved in, while Cynpym — which I think of as my main persona, the one I show people most often — has been hard to turn into a complete, larger project. I want to get back to it, because I think it can express things TRANCEDÆNCE simply can’t, but figuring out how to bring what I’ve learned from TRANCEDÆNCE into it, without collapsing the distinction between the two, is an ongoing problem. It might sound like an overly formal thing to worry about, but for me it’s a genuinely interesting one to solve. Photo by Anna Chaika courtesy of Artsvit Gallery Where are you currently based, and how has displacement—or, if you have remained in Ukraine, the transformation of everyday life there—affected the way you make and hear music? More broadly, what does identifying yourself as a Ukrainian artist mean to you now? Is “Ukrainian” primarily a cultural identity, a political position, a lived experience, or something that inevitably enters the sound itself? When the full-scale invasion started I moved back from Odesa to Dnipro, where I still live. For the first months it was mostly about getting all shit together – finding a new job, moving to a new place, making new connections. I didn’t really start thinking about my career again until I went to some of the first post-invasion gigs, some of which I was invited to perform at in late 2022. It was a really strange and transactional period – I see that the community wanted to continue functioning on the same logic and principles as it was before the war, not yet knowing how exactly the scene should transform. I had no idea either – but performing, and reminding myself I was still a musician, mattered a lot. With that mindset I released my second album …&2, which tried to capture that odd, liminal year. I’m not especially proud of it sonically, but I’m glad I made it — it kept me moving forward through a context that had changed completely since February 2022. Time passed and it became more obvious that initial enthusiasm for creating musical events in a pre-war fashion was fading away, at least in Dnipro. The cultural space felt colder and emptier as the first blackouts and Shahed attacks started. I stopped thinking seriously about music for a while — it felt impossible to fit back into the scene without some kind of reinvention. That changed when I went to Kyiv for a 20ft Radio event where Oleksii Podat was playing alongside other experimental and radical artists. Watching a crowd vibe to something that loud and harsh made me think that if I got back into music, there’d actually be an audience for it. That pushed me to put together my first real portfolio, get my old material onto streaming, and start applying to open calls — which eventually led to me being included on the ШЩЦ3 VA compilation, which was a huge deal for me as it got a lot of publications and I admired this label long before making experimental music myself. From there I started more new projects, met more local artists, worked with more Ukrainian art organizations, and did my first residencies. Becoming a direct participant in the Ukrainian underground scene, rather than an outside observer of it, was the biggest change in how I make music. I used to think of my work as representing more global subcultures and networks; now I keep in mind that I represent my local context too, and it’s basically impossible to separate my solo work from the Ukrainian people I’ve collaborated with. Whatever I pick up from elsewhere, I try to bring back and share with the local community as a priority. That’s not always simple — sometimes the local focus feels imposed by institutions, and the community itself keeps shifting and radicalizing politically — but caring about how my work resonates here, and about making something that matters to these specific people, has pushed me to try new mediums, work with new themes, and be more sincere as an artist. As for “Ukrainian” as a label — I think it’s an ongoing process of figuring out what we can be and do, not a fixed or essentialist thing, and I’m wary of romanticizing it. It’s an active practice, where we constantly adapt as a community for the sake of our own survival. It’s a lived experience people gain from cultural code, passport, language, land, contribution to community, etc. A lot of people carry “ukrainity” in different amounts, and for some it grows large enough to shape their whole way of living. Right now, being Ukrainian often means direct action and direct connection — we tend to self-organize without waiting for guidance from above. Turning “Ukrainian” into that kind of flexible, dispersed network, using whatever tools we have, is what we’re doing right now so that we can’t be crushed. Your earlier work repeatedly imagines the future: 0ne refers to technological singularity and “Coming of Age”, while Trip Reserved describes events acquiring meanings only later in life. Are you still able to think about the future in those terms? After more than four years of full-scale war, is imagining a future an artistic necessity, a luxury, an act of resistance—or something that has become almost impossible? I touched on part of this already — to summarize, I still find Mark Fisher’s Acid Communism and Capitalist Realism the most useful frame for thinking about the future, and I’m genuinely glad to see him getting more popular with younger audiences. It’s almost impossible to picture a realistic, positive future right now, but letting yourself start dreaming again feels like the necessary first step toward one. I can’t talk about the future without acknowledging how much has changed over the last few years — new technology, the political climate of USA-China and their world influence, COVID. Since the full-scale invasion, accelerationism feels like the most relevant frame to me globally. Even inside Ukraine, the new shape of drone warfare wasn’t something anyone expected, and its effect on our society and culture is hard to overstate. How we resist, how our trauma is shaped, how we fight and understand this war — all of that is being formed by new technology and new media. The faster we understand how it’s changing us, the better we adapt and the better we do strategically. The accelerationist view can be genuinely frightening given what a lot of theorists predict — especially with the current Trump administration having real roots in Dark Enlightenment thinking. It’s a fact that the tech sector today is largely controlled by people with no real interest in solving the world’s problems or improving people’s lives, and yet the technology keeps developing at full speed regardless. Most political parties, most of the public, even a lot of artists, underestimate or ignore this, while authoritarian regimes are already putting it to use. As an artist I feel a responsibility to engage with this, especially from a Ukrainian angle. I see Ukraine as a place where the future is actively unfolding — not just in terms of which weapons and technologies get used in this war, but in how the war and its outcome will reshape how we understand colonialism, imperialism, and globalism in a world with mass-deployed AI. Ukrainians have been living in that mode for a long time already: we’ve had some of the fastest, cheapest, least censored internet around; most of our schools and universities never fully left remote learning after COVID; we’ve gotten so used to working through blackouts that it’s less disruptive than people might expect. That’s how this society ended up more technologically acknowledged than a lot of much wealthier countries, under some of the worst possible conditions — which I find genuinely inspiring. I think younger Ukrainians are even better positioned to use technology culturally, and if we want to theorize seriously about a better future, we need to pay attention to what they’re actually doing, feeling, and thinking. I doubt many of them care much about experimental or contemporary art in the white-cube highbrow form that still dominates the field. A lot of art mediums and music genres are going to lose relevance fast if we don’t reshape them for younger artists who grew up with technology from birth — otherwise they’ll just go to virtual platforms instead. The same goes for “new money”: IT workers, e-scammers, crypto traders have real potential to become the next Ukrainian elite, so it’s worth starting that conversation now if we want Ukrainian art to have a future worth building. Honestly, these days I see more potential in Instagram Reels brainrot memes than in most institutional art projects, which too often feel technophobic and commodified — not exactly the right configuration for building something better. From debut performance in Odesa Finally, rather than asking you to define Ukraine, could you build a small portrait of the country as it exists for you right now: what book, film, artwork, monument or building, dish, meme, album and individual song best represent contemporary Ukraine—and why? I would choose ‘тсн’ by kissesfromeldar – but honestly, any of their recent releases would be a great fit. That music gives me the most hope about where Ukrainian music is going, and it represents Ukraine the way I want it represented: sincere, vulnerable, queer-coded, post-ironic, cutting-edge, visionary, self-referential, anti-institutional, and still respectful of its roots. I see how this music would be enjoyed equally by Ukrainians and foreigners. I think Ukrainians and foreign listeners can enjoy it equally, for different reasons — for us it’s full of context and references only we’d fully catch, while for people outside Ukraine it just sounds fresh, with very few real equivalents elsewhere. Those are the same qualities I’ve always valued in Svitlana Nianio’s music. kissesfromeldar isn’t based in Ukraine but performs around Europe, which also matters to me — having artists who matter equally to people who stayed and people who left because of the war feels important at a moment when those two groups keep drifting further apart.   SEPTEMBER 2, 2026 – KHARKIV sofiia khedekel Hi Sofiia, could you tell us about your musical background and how Соня Хедекель [Sofiia Khedekel] began as a project? What music were you listening to when you first started writing and recording, and how did you arrive at the combination of intimate vocals, dream-pop atmosphere and much denser guitar textures that characterises songs such as “Незупинно” and “Unison”? When I was a child, I studied at a music school for a few years, but eventually chose visual art instead. I had been writing music for a long time, mostly for myself – as a kind of personal diary. Gradually, I started sharing it publicly. I wouldn’t really call myself a “project” in the traditional sense: I don’t have a strategy or a team. I just honestly do what I feel an inner impulse to do. I started performing solo at local events in Kharkiv in 2025. But I always wanted a fuller sound, not just the format of keys and vocals. I have a fairly clear feeling of what I want to express, so it is important for me to control most of the process myself. This motivated me to learn guitar, music software and gradually build a small home setup for recording. I don’t connect myself to any particular genre and I don’t have very clear references. But obviously, what I listen to influences me: shoegaze, dream-pop, underground and lo-fi aesthetics. In my own sound, I care about a feeling of real human presence, melancholic haze and the texture I create by layering vocals and guitars. I’m glad you noticed this in your question. I work with music as an emotional space and I’m not really interested in making a quick impression – it’s more important to me that the sound pulls you in and exists as a certain state. If I am not mistaken, you live in Kharkiv, a city that has experienced more than four years of war and remains under frequent attack. How has living there changed since 2022, both personally and as a musician? Is it possible to adapt to that degree of uncertainty, and what are the particular difficulties of trying to write, record, perform and maintain an ordinary cultural life in Kharkiv at the moment? Yes, I live in Kharkiv. Sometimes it is difficult for me to answer the question “how has life changed”, because I feel like I’m starting to forget what life was like before the full-scale invasion, and that scares me. But of course, reality has a strong influence both on the topics I work with and on my approach to creativity in general. In some way, it may be a way for me to process and understand my own emotions and experiences. I have also become much less afraid of imperfection. It feels like, after everything that has happened, it is harder to scare me with things that used to make me feel vulnerable. There is quite a friendly music community in Kharkiv – we try to support each other. At the same time, it is quite small, as many people have left, so it can be difficult to find venues and people with whom you can create something together and move in the same direction. Of course, reality also affects the technical side of making music. For example, I recorded “Незупинно” during a period of severe power cuts after russian attacks. During the day I would go to a café to work, and in the evening, while I had a few hours of electricity at home, I would charge my laptop and record music in Ableton until the battery ran out. I did this sitting in the kitchen by candlelight. I think one day I will remember that period as something surreal. While writing the answer to this question, I remembered how I used to wait for the explosions to stop before starting to record vocals. At the time, I didn’t even think much about it. Now I realize how abnormal our reality has become. There is an interesting tension between your two recent singles. In “Незупинно” you describe the desire for an “emotional escape from reality” while remaining anxiously attached to it; in “Unison”, home becomes something you can find through trust and mutual understanding with another person. The city itself becomes almost weightless as everything seems to dissolve around the two people. Are these songs connected for you? Has your understanding of what “home” means changed through the experience of living in Kharkiv during the war? Yes, these songs are definitely connected – for me, they are two stages of how I am processing everything that is happening. “Незупинно” is probably about accepting that sometimes I simply can’t cope. In Ukrainian society, it can feel shameful to talk about this, because there will always be someone whose situation is much worse. Through this song, I wanted to get rid of that feeling of shame and give myself permission to talk about my own pain. About the desire to get rid of it, at least for a while. At that time, I started having thoughts about emigration, which I still sometimes come back to and which makes me feel sad. These thoughts also made me realize how much I value sincere things about my home, and how lost I might feel without it. It’s strange to love your home and still sometimes want to escape from it. “Унісон”, on the other hand, was written out of a desire to cultivate something in opposition to pain and destruction – something humanistic, something I really value. I feel that these are the things that keep me going now: the people close to me, understanding and sincere communication between us. After writing this song, I even allowed myself to fall in love, because I started trying not to run away from emotions – neither the bad ones or the good ones. So yes, both songs are about home for me. About two opposite feelings I have towards it at the same time: I love it with all my heart, but sometimes I also feel deeply tired and hopeless. Maybe home has stopped being just a specific place for me. It is both the pain connected to it and, at the same time, something tender, meaningful, and deeply personal. Your lyrics rarely describe current events directly, yet exhaustion, fear, disappearing traces, confused calendars, sleeplessness and the hope for a quiet night inevitably acquire particular meanings in contemporary Ukraine. Do you consciously leave that space open for the listener? Do you ever feel a responsibility as a Ukrainian artist to address the war explicitly, or can writing about intimacy, abstraction, anxiety and everyday life itself be a way of documenting what it feels like to live through this period? My lyrics are quite abstract because I naturally tend to think in images. And yes, this is my way of documenting my own experience, emotions and states rather than specific events. In general, creativity is more of a monologue for me than a way to communicate something to the outside world. But of course, I’m happy to find people who connect with what I do. I don’t feel a particular responsibility to speak about the war directly, because music is almost the only space where I can let go of any external responsibility and simply be honest with myself. I think journalists and reporters are the ones who directly document the war. While I document what it feels like to live in my reality, where many other parts of life exist alongside the war. If you had to build a small cultural portrait of Ukraine as it feels to you right now, what would you choose as one book, one film, one song, one album, one play, one artwork, one dish, one building, one monument and one meme — and why those particular choices? This question is difficult for me to answer because I feel like some time must pass before I can look at all of this from the outside. Right now, I still don’t fully understand what Ukraine is today or how I could describe it through specific cultural images. It feels like such a broad and complicated topic. Maybe a few years ago I could have given a more specific answer. But during this time, I have changed, my perception of what is happening has changed, and, as a result, my perception of Ukraine has changed too. So for now, I am still looking for these answers for myself. At the same time, I increasingly feel how unhealthy and distorted our idea of what is “normal” is becoming, while society itself is becoming traumatized. A lot of my attention is focused on this now, and it hurts me. But Ukraine is not only about the war and its consequences. It is also about its authenticity, mentality, landscapes, smells, people, and many other things that are difficult to fit into a single portrait. Maybe that is why I’m not ready yet to choose just one symbol for each of these categories.   SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 – SUMY Kateryna Pavlovska Having previously covered the Sumy-based label Bondeni, Pavlovska is a familiar name to readers of UFN. Her first solo release provides the perfect opportunity to reconnect. Hi Kateryna, “Veselo” is your first solo single after your work as the vocalist of ZzuppamanN and Tvaryny. Why did this particular song feel like the right moment to step forward under your own name? Does beginning a solo project give you a different kind of freedom—or responsibility—in terms of what you want to say and how personally you can say it? We decided to start with “Veselo” because this song opens my upcoming EP Vidpustka, setting the state of mind and atmosphere that makes you want to escape as quickly as possible to the warm waves of the sea, delicious food, and wine. The EP is closed, by the way, by the recently released song “Crete”. As for what will be between these two songs, we’ll keep that a secret for now. It’s also hard to say at this point exactly when the album will be finished and released. Actually, a little earlier I had already released the song “Jack” together with Tvaryny, where I wrote most of the lyrics and melodies, and on the song “Animal Instinct” I was a co-writer of the lyrics, which is why you can see the “feat.” credit with my name there. The thing is, there is no strict division of roles regarding the label’s projects at Bondeni. Yes, Tvaryny is Ihor Kostyk’s brainchild, ZzuppamanN is entirely under the control of Hryhorii Vashchenkov, Art Sopin is self-explanatory from the name, which is an abbreviated first and last name, while the notorious blogger CHUV is slowly but surely saving up for a studio to record his already legendary nine or ten albums. But at the same time, we really are primarily a community of musician friends who are always ready to help each other bring creative ideas to life. That’s why I sometimes write things for Tvaryny and help Hryhorii with his madness in ZzuppamanN, while Ihor Kostyk and CHUV have taken on the role of producing the project named after me. I don’t feel any overwhelming responsibility because everything I sing about is the reality that I and my friends live in. So, at the same time, I feel completely free. “Veselo” grew out of the news that another friend had been killed, yet the response was not a lament but a profanity-laced, almost absurdly cheerful song—the idea of laughing so as not to cry. After four and a half years of full-scale war, has humour become increasingly important as a way of processing what is happening around you? And what has changed most profoundly in the way you experience everyday life since February 2022? Yes, in terms of its meaning, “Veselo” is more of a personal song for Ihor, about his losses, although all of us have experienced loss. That’s why he even sings it together with me. And “Crete” is basically a kind of nostalgia for his vacation during the COVID-19 era, which you can see in the video for the song. But I completely share the emotions and thoughts he put into these songs, so singing about all of this felt completely natural to me. Both songs also contain that very specific kind of humor that has allowed all of us to keep living and creating over the past few years. In fact, the entire label’s creative output is permeated with it, because the creation of most of our songs starts with some kind of inside joke. It’s just done more directly here than, for example, in Tvaryny or Art Sopin. Yes, I’m talking about profanity and distinctly Ukrainian swearing. There was actually a rather sweet moment with “Veselo” when the guys somewhat awkwardly asked whether I was comfortable singing lyrics like that. Apparently, they had forgotten that I had already recited an absolutely catastrophic amount of swearing in ZzuppamanN’s manifesto “Idoly”. After that, everything else seems like child’s play. As for changes in the way I perceive everyday life, I can say just one thing: you start appreciating your family, friends, and creativity more and more, because without them, getting through this kind of “everyday life” is incredibly difficult.   SEPTEMBER 5, 2026 – CHERNIHIV Fedir Tkachov Hi Fedir, it’s been a while! When we spoke back in September 2022, you described improvisation as fundamental to the way you make music, something you partly inherited from your father, and said that the full-scale invasion had given you an urgency to leave behind a substantial body of work. Four years later, Uncut Jams is built from relatively spontaneous synthesizer explorations, while your new Legacy Series is deliberately returning to older recordings that might otherwise have remained unheard. Has your relationship with improvisation and with your own musical archive changed during those four years? A lot of water has flown since 2022. My core way of working “create a beautiful sound and try to improvise some beautiful music with it” hasn’t changed. But within that I feel like I had a lot of growth, even if that’s not something I can quantify or explain with words. I still feel the urgency to leave behind more music, both newly made and oldies. That’s the best I can offer the world, and at this point my life doesn’t have much meaning outside of that. And what made the 2016 cello improvisation “Warnings” feel particularly relevant to release in 2026, when you now hear in it “warnings from the past” about events you could not then have imagined? I’ve been making music for many years, but I only started releasing it more or less seriously in 2022. “Warnings” used to be a nameless file that surprised me every time I would dive into my older recordings and projects. It has that weird mix of urgency and mourning. It was a perfect choice to start my “Legacy Series”, because it’s a cello recording, which was the instrument that really lured me into the world of music making, and it was strong enough to stand on its own as a single. Not every release needs a story, but I find that humans seem to better connect with music that way, and I came up with a story of It being a misunderstood and ignored warning about the future invasion and darkness it brought with it. There was nothing particularly relevant to release it in 2026, other than a feeling it was time to do so, and to finally give way for other neglected music I have in store. Uncut Jams is interesting because you explicitly say you weren’t trying to demonstrate your abilities or construct a major conceptual statement—you were playing with instruments, having fun and sometimes using music as a refuge from pain. Yet you also say that removing those expectations led you towards compositional structures and sounds that you might normally have rejected as too excessive or complex. Has “not overthinking” become an increasingly important part of your practice? I don’t overthink some things and badly overthink others. For example, I like live-recorded improvisations because it condenses the aspects of composition and production into this singular realtime process, and by the end of the performance you either got it or not. It’s quite an honest way of making music. Even if I use modern technology to do that, I still have only two hands and a certain level of musical ability. At the same time, I have a relatively conceptual album project that I’ve been dragging for years, refining the concept, changing the name, adding and removing music. Just a couple of weeks ago I recorded a piece that feels like a fitting last track for it, but I’m having a hard time to apply the “no overthinking” mindset and workflow to the rest of it, as some compositions are either too complex or carry too much pain. It’s a heavy album, hopefully I have enough time to finish it. Ultimately, I treat live-recorded and produced music as two separate sonic art forms. I really love both, and I just had a new release, spiritually similar to Uncut Jams, but focused on acoustic cello improvisations. Listening back to pieces such as “Captains’ Quarters”, “Cyber Jungle”, “Daily Triumphs” and “Everything Ends Eventually”, can you hear circumstances from late 2025 entering the music despite your decision not to make the album explicitly about them? Life events and experiences inevitably inform and even bleed into my creative work, that’s a fact. With some compositions it’s quite subtle or almost non-existent, with others it gets very personal. Honestly, I wouldn’t want it any other way. In the age of so called AI and everything becoming increasingly more fake, at least I can say “Based on real events” haha) Back in 2022 you mentioned your cousin Danny as someone who had supported your music long before you were really sharing it publicly and who helped expand your musical tastes. Now that relationship has resurfaced as Thrasher Grace, but the three pieces on the album actually document an earlier period when you had limited equipment, slow computers and much less technical experience: Daniil’s voice becomes the raw material of “Mindstorm”, his eBow guitar generates “Uncertain Times”, and “Meadow” comes from an improvisation involving guitar, a smartphone used as a MIDI keyboard and a Korg controller. Why did you decide to preserve and release these recordings rather than remake them with the resources and experience you have now? “Legacy Series” is about honouring and presenting the older works as they are. I slightly remastered the audio to hopefully provide a better listening experience, but I really respect the music that I did in the past and I wouldn’t release it if that wasn’t the case. On top of that, I don’t really care about remakes. But reworking old material into something completely new is always interesting, like treating a track as a sample pack to build a new sonic narrative, which I explore sometimes. Maybe I’ll need another series of releases for that kind of thing. And does Thrasher Grace represent an archival project celebrating your shared musical past, or has rediscovering this material made you and Daniil want to create something new together? I feel I can say for both of us that properly releasing this music definitely inspired us to make something new. There’s no knowing what future Thrasher Grace might sound like, but we have plenty of instruments at our disposal, and we both have grown exponentially as musicians over the years, even if in considerably different dimensions. It’s only about us getting serious and doing the work. When we last spoke, you had only recently returned to Chernihiv after being displaced during the siege, and you described not knowing when you left in March 2022 whether you would ever see your home or family again. More than four years into the full-scale invasion, what is everyday life in Chernihiv like now, and how has your relationship with the city changed since that experience? It’s quite surreal to say this, but in retrospect that time right after the 2022 siege was quite blissful, there was a lot more hope in the air. For a few months back then life has seemed to return to a version of normal. I was also quite happy in my personal life, I was in love and probably was loved back. I’m almost nostalgic about it. Things only went downhill from there, but also a lot more nuance and depth about the war and the world has been revealed. These days the city is almost constantly in the air raid mode, and the density and success rate of the attacks seems to be increasing. It’s not a safe place to be. Upcoming winter will most likely be quite bleak, to put it mildly. But regardless if we’ll have water and heat or not, I have enough battery-powered devices to keep creating, at least for a while. In 2022 you were still able to speak about gratitude, remaining functional and building a future for yourself as an artist. Are you still able to think about the future in those terms today, and has living in Chernihiv throughout these intervening years changed what you want music — and your life as a musician — to be? It’s hard to choose an appropriate lens for this question, but maybe a few different truths can coexist. It’s not all doom and gloom, after all I was able to keep myself in one piece so far, and even in 2026 I consider myself to be blessed in many ways. But I’m 36 now, and I realise that the likelihood of me seeing 40 is quite low. I try to keep a positive outlook on life, but I live a day at the time, and any kind of future planning feels naive and futile. Considering the current trajectory of events, my best hope is making music a little while longer without any big dreams or expectations. At the same time, I appreciate my life’s story for what it is and has been so far, a really nice ride. 2026 was quite a fruitful year for me in terms of releasing music and streaming live performances, and I hope to keep and ramp up the pace going forward. Cello Drones brings you back to the instrument that, as you write, “lured” you into music more than half your life ago. The cello remains very recognisable throughout the six pieces, even as looping allows individual gestures to accumulate into drones and increasingly layered textures. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Ukrainian artists have had to work in circumstances in which their nationality and the war can become almost unavoidable contexts through which their work is perceived. What will we feel when the explosions and gunfire fall silent, when we look at our scorched land and realise that it is truly over? It is almost a narrative from the perspective of an observer who is looking back at everything that has happened – the hardship, the losses, the destruction – from a point at which the war is finally over. For me, it is a kind of silent contemplation of that experience, but at its centre there is also a deep hope and belief that, with time, wounds can heal. To imagine such a postlude while the war is still continuing is, in itself, a way of looking beyond the present moment and holding on to the possibility of an ending, of peace and of healing. They are very different symbols, but together they connect something deeply everyday and familiar with the cultural memory and beauty of the city I come from.   SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 – KYIV photo by Anna Reznik Forma Formanta Could you begin by telling us about your musical background and how Forma Formanta came into being? Zahid was recorded between Vienna and Kyiv from 2021 to 2025, spanning the period immediately before and after Russia’s full-scale invasion. You describe it as reflecting the loss of a foundation or axis — something that might be called “home” — while also connecting that feeling to a wider state of turbulence and increasing entropy. It’s not exactly a new thought. The material written during those years started to contain more motifs of endings, finality, and completion. Maybe the only difference is that I tried to push them into something even rawer, noisier, and more careless than is usually considered acceptable. Apart from that, I used the Soviet TOM 1501 synthesizer on almost every track. It has this very broad and deep string sound which, for me personally, is already associated with something pleasant and forgotten (and no, I don’t mean the usual nostalgia about ice cream costing five kopeeks or anything like that). The intent and the meaning, Raw forces, twin states.   Peshka ~ Fatebreak / Raw Void While I’m trying to figure out how to fill a God-sized hole in my soul, I decided to release a few more tracks from a past version of myself.   Alla Zagaykevych ~ Vyshyvanyi “Kyiv. Summer. War. War, war – endless war. Glissando of sirens tearing the air. They are the loudest now. Unless the great Lavra bell is louder than them. Every morning at nine o’clock it fills the city with its powerful, pure voice like the sea. But the sirens return. Insidiously. At night and during the day. In the morning at dawn. The cruel, unnatural sound of war arrhythmia. I can tell the story of our time with lines from the opera “Vyshyvanyi”, with the lyrics of its heroes. “This war has been going on for too long to only think about it” – sings the Girl in a duet with Vyshyvanyi… “we must build while there is still a chance… especially since who knows how long this war will last” – and these are the nervous answers of Colonel Bolbochan. While working on the opera “in pre-war times” (the opera was written in 2019 and staged in October 2021 at the Kharkiv Opera Theater), I was, of course, exclusively concerned with artistic challenges. How to convey the special nerve of Serhiy Zhadan’s poetry through “operatic” means? How to combine the “hero’s expression” with almost adolescent naked sensuality in the part of Vyshyvanyi? How to build a musical dramaturgy around mainly of wartime events… After all, all the events in the opera are somehow connected with the war – the Great (First World War), the liberation struggles of Ukraine for independence. Even the most tender scene with cadets from the youth of Wilhelm von Habsburg is a metaphorical “premonition” of war – the expectations of a cold and terrible winter. After all, how to convey the feeling of a layered consciousness, the “fragility of reality” in the opera, because the main character constantly travels between worlds in his delusions during interrogations in the Lukyanivka prison… The musical language of the opera is consciously saturated with elements of the “fragile” aesthetics initiated by Berg and Schoenberg. A variety of vocal forms, including combinations of modern academic extended techniques and folk vocals, a wide palette of orchestral sonoristic means, including spectral techniques, and finally electroacoustic sounds and electronic processing of the orchestra and voices in real time, are components that ensured the continuous “variability” of the musical language, the rapid change of the opera’s tebro-texture. “About war”, about struggle, about love, beauty, about our dreams, our no less complex and fragile reality, I seem to continue to speak in the language of “Vyshyvanyi”… Among the sirens. In a half-sleep. Therefore – loudly. Therefore – tenderly.” – Alla Zagaykevych, Kyiv, 2026   Mootney ~ What Happened To The Music David Mootney, hailing from the outskirts of Ukraine’s capital, has always sought to blur the boundaries between genres, bringing a rebellious spirit and an uncompromising philosophy to his craft. The aesthetics of the “dirty Kyiv electro” tradition have remained a defining thread throughout his work. But the only constant is change, and the music evolves alongside us. What Happened To The Music? is both a personal reflection and a question directed outward. Where do we go from here? How do we confront the consequences of endless consumption? Expanding on ideas introduced in his previous Mystictrax release, Mootney takes a radically different approach. Instead of aiming to overwhelm or shock, he chooses subtlety, drawing the listener in rather than demanding attention. Built around extensive vinyl sampling, the EP blends euphoric, mystical and faintly delirious melodies with fractured electro rhythms. Across three original tracks, Mootney explores the outer edges of electro, while a heavyweight remix from PROGRAMM_LDN co-founder D3U5E adds an extra dose of raw energy to close the release.   Piriinka ~ Помітки Помітки is a mini-album of seven notes in which I searched for the diversity of life through music for five years. Here I leave intersections from dreamy to painful questions related to self-knowledge and growing up.   Tetiana Khoroshun ~ Yalos Yalos—γιαλος, meaning “shore” in Greek—is a collection of electroacoustic works by Tetiana Khoroshun that explores Ukraine’s landscapes in relation to water. The journey begins with the Chongar salt flats and the piece *Crimean Titan*—a 2018 recording of crossing the illegal border with Crimea, combined with a chance audio recording, which together form a performative, documentary noise piece. The journey continues with the piece *Madrigal*—an octaphonic ensemble ritual marking the return of the Sukha Moskovka River to its natural course, navigating the vast scale of the sound processes at the Zaporizhstal plant and entering into a complex relationship of coexistence, resistance, and memory with the industrial landscape. The third part—LJ—immerses the listener in the waters of the Black Sea. Here, the sea appears not as a backdrop or a symbol of tranquility, but as a living and dangerous force capable of simultaneously holding, moving, and destroying: “Just like in …, basically, if you don’t know how to swim, it can simply destroy you—it’ll just grab you and throw you against the seabed, because not everyone knows how to swim there…”   Khladna Landscape ~ Lichtgestalten A cathartic sound as a manifestation of infinity. This single is about neutrality, about perceiving the world and experience as it is. Waves of shimmering words, memories, everything that has shaped the human experience over millennia. All of this is one vast vortex, penetrating the very depths of humanity, which ultimately is humanity. This single is about the I-am, about the state of not being, of existing only as a manifestation.   Regina Collage ~ Horizont Ukrainian artist Regina Collage’s new album ‘Horizont’ is a personal and honest document of rebuilding a life and creative voice in Bristol. The record holds space for themes of burnout, quiet shame, tenderness and the courage of staying emotionally open when the world feels unstable. Feeling carries the songs forward. Across bedroom recordings and borrowed studios, Regina moves between cloudy dissonance and stark minimal arrangements built around bass, fragments of guitar, and an exposed voice. The album takes its name from the Ukrainian word for “horizon,” that unreachable line where sky meets earth. For Regina, the horizon became a quiet metaphor for living with distance and uncertainty. Inspired by one of her collage artworks showing a figure lying in grass and staring toward that far line, the title track reflects a feeling of moving toward something that never quite comes closer. “It is important for me to speak about Ukraine and remind people that the war has not ended,” Regina says. “Some of my friends are fighting and some are still making music. They were musicians before the invasion and everything changed for them. My hometown Kharkiv is under constant attack. My parents are there. Even if it is not always in the news, it is happening every day. I also want to represent our underground music culture. I love the music from Ukraine and the people making it.”   ROSS KHMIL ~ KAILAS SUNRISE live recorded outsider power trance music originaly released as a mix for examine-archive platform   Sasha Chemerov & Hidden Element ~ Все Це Колись Мине [All This Will Pass Someday] The release becomes a quintessential reflection of contemporary surrealism, where uplifting, life-affirming music collides with stark social realist poetry, creating a powerful contrast between hope and the reality of the present. In addition to the original version, the release also includes an instrumental version and a live recording from Hidden Element’s performance at Brave!Factory Festival 2026.   Various Artists 1 ~ The Freya Files A Darkwave Compilation in Support of Ukraine She rides into battle cloaked in dusk and gold. The Freya Files (and its brother release The Odin Files) was never meant to be an easy release. As part of a 37-track project, the compilation faced legal obstacles, political pressure we never expected to encounter in 2026, failed hard drives, lost files, production delays, and repeated setbacks that threatened to stop it from ever reaching the public. It survived because the reason behind it mattered more to us than the obstacles. Rooted in the darkwave, electro, EBM, and industrial underground, The Freya Files brings together female artists whose music moves between beauty and defiance, grief and determination, restraint and force. Each track stands on its own, but every contribution serves the same purpose: supporting Ukraine in its fight for sovereignty, dignity, and survival. The release became a testament to resilience. Every recovered recording, rebuilt session, resolved dispute, and refusal to give in became part of its history. Freya, goddess of war and love and chooser of the fallen, represents those who carry sorrow without allowing it to silence them. These artists transform that sorrow into sound: fierce, radiant, synthetic, and unbroken. Proceeds will support humanitarian and frontline aid efforts in Ukraine. 🜁 For the mourners. 🜂 For the mothers. 🜃 For those who dance among the ruins   an honest fox ~ The Weight Of Empty Cities Part III: Horizon   Volodymyr Tkachov ~ Soundscapes “Soundscapes” Part 1-5 were recorded at home studio in 2001.Equipment used for recording is – Jolana Special (electric guitar) – kids toys – MD-57 microphone – Vega 122c tape recorder – bathroom sink, shower and some bathroom accesories. Note on the hidden part of the cassette booklet says “To my patient family”   Cryptic Chorus ~ And the wheels of war keep creaking This album was recorded in the pauses between combat missions in a real war. That’s why it took so long to record. This album is somewhat different from my previous works — on it, I tried to express more of my emotions and personal experiences. I hope you enjoy it.   corn wave ~ elephant entertainment Reissue of the 2023 release with updated cover art and bonus tracks.   Decorodi ~ Topography   Ніщо ~ Каркоза [СТУС-079] The second album by the band ніщо [nіshcho / nothing], which, as it unfolds, tells the story of a man who is given a second chance at life after committing suicide. He tries to readjust to the realities of the modern world. His attempts prove futile, and in his isolation he gradually loses his mind, becoming convinced that all the horrors of the world around him are manifestations of an emerging new world order. He calls it Каркоза [Carcosa]. In the end, his delusions turn out to be real…   Neroba ~ Pechersk Neroba is not a person. Neroba is the name left behind after the person disappears. People in Ukraine say, “This one is a Neroba,” or “This was done by Neroba” — нероба, literally a slacker, a lazy man. Nobody remembers meeting him. Some say he was responsible for early LAN fileshares in Obolon that no longer exist. Others say Neroba is a local demon inhabiting underpasses, relay cabinets and service corridors beneath the city. Our protagonist, Neroba, was part of Da Sintezatoros!, a duo from the young Kyiv electronic scene of the 90s and among the first groups to introduce experimental techno in independent Ukraine. Later, producing music for TV ads and commercial jingles, and tracks for Ukrainian pop and independent artists, Neroba slowly accumulated a catalogue of works where his name wasn’t prominent. The music on this album was created in his bedroom studio between 2010 and 2020. A blend of boogie, funk, house and disco – 12-bit drums programmed on his beloved Casio RZ-1, alongside the usual suspects: a Roland JV-1080 and a Yamaha DX7, a couple of drum machines and a cheap early-90s Boss SE-50 stereo effects unit. Neroba’s small synth sanctuary translated the mood of the city at a specific hour. The artist currently lives in Kyiv. We are happy to present his debut solo work. This album is by Neroba.   Motorpig ~ We Inherited the Ruins We Inherited the Ruins Things are made slowly. Wood is polished. Surfaces are worn down. Instructions become meaningless. The archive burns. Somewhere beneath it all, the machinery continues to hum. A study in repetition, friction, manual labor, and whatever remains after progress has left the room.   Oleksii Podat ~ We Were Born To Feel Everything A long-form composition knitting sundry paraphernalia of intimate value into a tēla that feels as recognisable as it is unhinged — akin to the stroke of a reliable brush tilting just enough to unveil the mesh of the fabric, only to skid into another aberrant tangle.   Doctor Bugg ~ REM REM – Rapid Eye Movement – is the phase of sleep during which a person dreams. In this state, reality feels fluid, surreal, and dissociated. Doctor Bugg explores REM through fragmented memories, a sense of lost time, and liminality. REM focuses on the instrumental canvas. The composition features percussive electronic sounds and jagged, disorienting textures that intertwine with guitar and processed saxophone recordings. With this release, the artist changes course, moving away from a focus on lyrics. Genre spectrum: industrial electronics, experimental hip hop, spoken word, and improvisation. “Listening is a very personal experience. It’s best to listen to this music without worrying about how it might be perceived by someone else” – prescribes Doctor Bugg.   Alex Malch ~ In a Landscape 5 years ago, in 2021, Alex started writing this album and after multiple unsuccessful attempts to record it I have finally finished the project This album has everything he wanted and needed to say, musically and lyrically, and he don’t intend to release any more solo music.   Vøvk, КАТ ~ Split (Live @ Druk, Kharkiv, 17.05.2026) This live split captures our joint performance by Vøvk and KAT, recorded live on May 17, 2026, at a show in Kharkiv organized by the KAZKA Family community. The release features four tracks: Vøvk presents ‘Sil’ and ‘Leleka’ from last year’s album ‘Litera’, while KAT contributes ‘Lyst’ and ‘Bez Pravyl’ – the latter recorded in Ukrainian for the very first time. For KAT, the evening was particularly meaningful, marking their first live performance in their hometown of Kharkiv in three years. “For years, we wanted to organize a show together with KAT, but for various reasons, it just never happened. When this spontaneous gig in Kharkiv came up, we decided to make the absolute most of it. The idea for the release came together quickly: we felt we had to capture this special day and time together. Especially in one of our absolute favorite cities.” — Vøvk We are releasing this split as a Bandcamp exclusive, available solely for streaming and purchase on the platform. All proceeds from sales will go directly to the ongoing fundraiser by the KAZKA Family community, supporting those who make events like this possible in the first place. “We always love playing alongside our friends in Vøvk, and this show happened completely spontaneously. Even though it was our first time performing in three years, we jumped at the opportunity to capture May ’26 in Kharkiv with this short live split. We want more than just dark memories to remain from these times; we want Kharkiv to stay alive and thriving. Intimate initiatives like this – which was Vøvk’s idea – are simply priceless.” — KAT   Serhii Litinskyi ~ Fernstimmen The musical practice common in the time of Ockeghem and Josquin has disappeared from our present-day musical protocols, in which the listener’s customary connection to music is organized linearly. This is symmetrical to the way in which music, in turn, connects to the listener. Today, it is difficult even to perceive the difference between these two connections, but once there was an enormous distance between them. A singer taking part in the performance of a Josquin Mass presupposed a trajectory of sound that did not lead to the listener, because the figure of the listener did not exist in the church in the first place. Even when members of the congregation were present at the service, the singers were either isolated from them or turned away from them; combined with the church’s powerful reverberant acoustics, this effectively deprived the congregation of the possibility of perceiving the music. If we set aside the liturgical function and the metaphysical dimension of the process, and consider instead the physical and physiological dimension of musical practice, music here returned to itself, existing in a reflexive loop. The sound produced by the singer returned to the singer and shaped a state in which he could produce sound that was even more effective at producing the state in which effective sound could be produced. The circular trajectory of the music enclosed and isolated the musical material. When we encounter Josquin’s music, we immediately register the autonomy and coherence of its sonic construction. In terms of expression, it is alien to the kind of expressivity we habitually describe as a reliance on an outward effect. When we listen to Josquin’s music today, we connect to it asymmetrically. The singers’ voices always seem to come, so to speak, from afar; they do not address us directly. We always listen from the side, in a sense eavesdropping, witnessing the circular trajectory of the music and the effect that sound, through the singer’s body, has upon itself. In working on this piece, I sought to reproduce this ancient circular trajectory of sound. This also determined the insufficiency, and ultimately the inadequacy, of a linear algorithm in which the score is realized in a single act: a direct performance, fixed in a recording and aimed at the listener. I needed to submit to the effect of the sound and, in turn, affect it under the influence of that effect. Having accepted these rules, in the course of realizing the piece in sound I substantially altered and supplemented the performance of the original score with sounds of different origins. In other words, I intervened in its realization by virtually every means through which a composer can directly influence the sonic result—from field recordings to sound samples, to the creation of autonomous musical structures and events within this new sonic environment. These almost always conceal the initial material, making it nearly indistinguishable within the texture of the final sound. Nevertheless, it was precisely this initial impulse, at the origin of the circular trajectory, that determined the character and rhythm in which the spiral of this music unfolds. I am sincerely grateful to all the musicians through whom Fernstimmen—“distant voices”—have come closer.   DJ POPS ~ между частотами The label ERYTHROLEUKOPLAKIA out of Kyiv presents itself in a raw, punky style, but this second album from associate DJ Pops is altogether more considered and delicate than you might be expecting. It’s another one with IDM/braindance irregularity at its core, but it’s definitely got more emphasis on the “dance” side of the equation; so no matter how lopsided the grooves might get, they nonetheless are grooves, and hold the attention and the body locked in. It also, however abstract it gets, feels weirdly un-digital—like constructions of wood, string, rusty metal, tape, and glue, sometimes with little creatures running around inside them. [Bandcamp Daily]   MIXES   VIEWING ROOM (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这是Ukrainian Field Notes系列第五十八期合辑性质的播客与乐评文章，聚焦乌克兰实验音乐场景。内容并非单一专辑评论，而是介绍多位乌克兰艺术家的新作，涵盖ambient、IDM、实验电子等多种风格，并辅以DJ混音与影像作品。亮点包括Side-Line Magazine的公益合辑、Vlad Fisun等电子音乐人的混音，以及Resonance FM播客中16岁哈尔科夫少女Daryna介绍残障儿童艺术工作室Aza Nizi Maza的内容。文章在战时背景下记录了乌克兰地下音乐的创作生态，兼具新闻性与音乐性，展现了独立场景在极端环境下的持续生命力。新人音乐人众多，风格跨度大，跨界融合明显，但因合辑性质，单一作品深度有限，整体偏向信息汇编。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are classic bands whose lineups become fixed in time, beyond any later variations, as the very ones through which we first discovered them; these are the lineups that produced a handful of classic albums, creating the impression (or illusion) that they could do no wrong. This happened with the Peter Gabriel-era Genesis in the 70s, with Yes during the time Bruford and Wakeman were in the band, and in many other cases, given that the decade was so rich and vast it seemed endless, and it happened with Roxy Music. However, what set Roxy Music apart was that, alongside Bryan Ferry, possessing a voice that was glamorous yet capable of sounding menacing when needed, and Andy Mackay (on sax and oboe, coaxing out an incredible sonic range), and Phil Manzanera (a guitarist who possessed undeniable credentials in an era when every self-respecting guitarist had to prove their worth), and Paul Thompson (on drums, anchoring a sextet with such great chemistry), there was Brian Eno. He was the element that would disrupt any sense of equilibrium, or, conversely, help them find balance within the very imbalance that made them unique."Re-Make / Re-Model" kicks off without asking for permission; Manzanera's guitar seems to attack, and the same goes for Ferry's vocals, almost punk before punk existed. They sounded frenetic, with McKay's sax channeling free jazz, and were expertly backed by Graham Simpson's bass. Brian Eno's signature backing vocals and synthesizer interventions were already present; he brought the electronics, he brought modernity. You can sense the freedom and the way they play around with interruptions (including a nod to the Beatles) during the pauses before the finale. Ferry was not just a singer with a distinct personality; he also contributed significantly on the piano with his dissonant notes. They had fun experimenting in the studio, and that spirit was captured on the record; the proof is that it sounds like a live album."Ladytron" opens with a space-rock feel; Mackay's oboe displays a subtlety echoed by Ferry, revealing a facet of the band completely different from the previous track. The sound then seems to shift toward the Canterbury scene, with the saxophone and guitar sharing the lead, at times epic, at others drifting aimlessly without vying for the spotlight. "If There Is Something" surprises with a country-western atmosphere, yet the band transforms it into glam rock in the vein of Bowie or Elton John; then, Manzanera's Black Sabbath-esque solo tears us away from the Wild West, while Ferry sings as only he could, at times reminiscent of Family's Roger Chapman."Virginia Plain" would become one of the band's classics from this early period, featuring the humor in Ferry's vocals combined with Eno's synthesizer work, all within a track that remained, at its core, rock 'n' roll in their own distinctive style: an avant-garde approach devoid of solemnity, which is precisely why we still love it so much.The wonderful thing about this debut was its variety; as we shifted to something more serious and experimental with "2HB," Ferry's voice transported us to space epics and evoked a yearning for a bohemian past, something he harbored even in his youth at the time, which also gave the band a modern edge. Paul Thompson varied the rhythms, introducing more syncopation, while the saxophone's intensity receded, leaving Eno's keyboards to persist, looping over and over, and making us feel as though we were inside Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.We are talking about space, and it feels as though we are plunging into a black hole of unknown destination; "The Bob (Medley)" kicks off, following the intro, with an epic rock sound driven by saxophones reminiscent of Van der Graaf Generator and Ferry's defiant vocals. Then comes a medieval section, echoes of the past, fitting for a band as cinematic as Roxy Music (especially during this era) followed by raw, wild rock, yet punctuated by synthesizers that feel like blocks of ice in the desert, alongside Mackay's frenetic oboe. And when Ferry's piano notes arrive, and the guitar soars like thunder in a storm, making its presence powerfully felt, we know this band is like no other."Chance Meeting" is one of those very special tracks that seem not to have been composed on Earth, possessing a strange beauty and a strange melody; it certainly resembles contemporary classical music, dissonant and asymmetrical, with an architecture that defies established conventions. This is because the piano and Ferry's calm, simmering vocals contrast with Manzanera's guitar, which cuts through the air like a power saw.If you think Would You Believe settles into calm and normalcy, you are mistaken; Ferry's obsession with nostalgia takes us, for the first time, though not the last, back to the 50s, but in a wild, street-level style."Sea Breezes" once again pushes the boundaries of the avant-garde with an Eastern-tinged melody where Ferry's voice takes center stage, shining like the marquee lights of an old theater in a seaside town where seagulls bear eternal witness to the people passing through year after year. The music conjures images and stirs emotions; it seems to repeat itself yet introduces subtle shifts, unfolding slowly, like the passing years, almost imperceptibly. Beneath the layers of wildness and impetuosity lay wisdom and deliberate structure; Paul Thompson knew exactly when to make his entrance, and just as the oboe plays a delicate melody, Manzanera cuts through it with his guitar, creating a harmony born of chaos. When Ferry sings, it is as if he is backed by a strange orchestra, strange, indeed, but an orchestra nonetheless.Precisely by downplaying an era that seemed to be growing increasingly serious, they conclude with a simple, almost a cappella melody titled "Bitter's End", a tune reminiscent of an old village, quintessentially English, fully aware that every avant-garde movement follows its own unique path.

items._cn_summary: Roxy Music首张专辑将华丽摇滚与前卫实验融为一体，Brian Eno的合成器介入与Andy Mackay的自由爵士萨克斯交织出不安的平衡。Bryan Ferry的钢琴以不和谐音为基底，Phil Manzanera的吉他兼具攻击性与史诗感，乐队在录音室中展现出类似现场即兴的活力与混乱美学。从太空摇滚质感、坎特伯雷派即兴到乡村西部元素的解构重塑，每首曲目都拒绝落入类型俗套。Eno的电子音效为整张专辑注入现代性与前卫性，使其超越同期大部分华丽摇滚作品，成为英伦实验流行音乐的重要起点。

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Undoubtedly one of the great surprises of this year is the release of King Gizzard's full-blown EDModyssey 'Alien Metal', which is their twenty-eight studio album to date. The follow-up to 2025's'Phantom Island' sees the Australian band abandoning all rock instrumentation for a futuristic beat-driven, techno-inspired rave sound, utilizing a modular synth system that allows them to explore avast range of sequenced rhythms, electronic textures, and an overall synthetic, club-orientedproduction style. Contemporary bands rarely do such dramatic stylistic shifts, but this acid-ladencreation from the kings of psychedelic blues turns out to be a fun and engaging listen (that willnevertheless shock many dedicated fans), that is above all else, a finely constructed electronicwork, wherein each tracks flows into the next one, giving the impression of a massive piece ofprogressive house. Within this mixture of quirky techno beats, bassy breakbeats, and ambientinterludes, the ominous alien-like robotic vocals that wiggle their way through, give 'Alien Metal'somewhat of a sci-fi edge. However, despite all of the pristine synth sequences and polished studiosound, the occasional repetitiveness of this album can potentially lead to listener fatigue.Moreover, the synthetic club feel provides for a great background listen, but is there really thatmuch substance to dig into upon repeated listens? The tracks that I enjoy the most on 'Alien Metal'are the punchy opener 'Sapience', which beautifully transitions into the excellent title track,followed by the powerful and mesmerizing 'Level 5', and the trippy 'Uqt', which appears towards theend. The album finale is strong, too, while the entire work feels intentionally futuristic andvibrant, which is perhaps what most listeners would cling to.

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online.
